voiceover.text: Picture a regional high school of eight hundred students that decides to support the goals. It paints the seventeen squares on a wall, runs an assembly, and raises fourteen hundred dollars for an overseas water charity. Students can now name several goals. Meanwhile, in the same town, about a third of students skip breakfast, the only bus to the youth health service runs twice a day, and the sportsground has no lights, so nothing happens after five in winter. Was the school's program worthwhile? And what could change something on that second list?

The goals were agreed by national governments, but the United Nations itself points out that most of the targets can't be reached without local government. Look at what a council controls: parks, pools and lighting, footpaths and crossings, planning near schools, libraries and youth spaces, community grants, and food and water safety. So localisation means adapting the goals to local priorities, and reporting local data against them. It runs both ways. Downwards, a council asks what the goals mean here. Upwards, it reports local results, and some Australian councils publish their own review.

So, the school. The fair verdict has two parts. Awareness has real value: students learned, the school signalled that these issues matter, and money went somewhere useful. But it changed nothing on the second list, and that's where its own students lose health. It treated the goals as a topic, not a tool. Awareness starts from the goals, and is measured by who turned up. Localisation starts from a local need, and is measured by change from a baseline. And labelling existing activity with goal numbers, when no decision changed, is called SDG-washing. The test is simple: would any decision have been different without the goals?

scenes.title: six steps from a need to a proposal

voiceover.text: Here's the method, and you start at step one, not step three. One: establish the need, with the community, and reach beyond the students already in sport or leadership. Two: name the goals it sits under, with mechanisms, not icons. Three: find the assets before the deficits: a hall, a club, a bus, a trusted organisation. Four: design across at least three Ottawa action areas, with who acts and roughly what it costs. Five: set a baseline and an indicator, reported for the groups most at risk. Six: say how it survives. The goals tell you what matters and how to measure it. The Charter tells you what kind of action to take.

Now run it on the town. With students, the need chosen is nowhere to be active after school in winter, and no way to reach the youth health service. The council lights the sportsground until eight pm, measured in hours of use. After advocacy, the transport authority adds two late-afternoon buses, measured by visits to the service from this town. A community organisation runs a breakfast program, checked against a baseline survey. A youth reference group gets a real budget and a vote. And a local club runs eight weeks of coaching, then keeps it going.

scenes.title: three features of a good proposal

voiceover.text: Three features make this proposal strong. Every row names who acts, and every one of them sits outside the school: the council, a transport authority, a community organisation, a club. That's health in all policies, locally. And every measure sits above activity on the impact staircase. Lights installed is activity; hours of use is output; visits and breakfasts eaten are behaviour. None claims a health outcome yet. And two rows are built to outlive the funding: the coaching passes to a club, and the reference group gets a standing place. That's why it would still exist in three years.

scenes.title: the strategy checklist, applied to your own proposal

voiceover.text: Before you submit a proposal, run the strategy checklist you've been building. Four lines you know. Who decided? If young people were surveyed but had no vote, that's consultation. Who does it reach, and who does it miss? Programs run through schools and clubs miss young people who've left both. What changes, and how would you know: a baseline, an indicator, results by group? And what survives the funding? Two lines are new. Who acts outside health? And is this the biggest thing you could do, or just the easiest? Lighting a ground is popular. Changing a bus timetable isn't, and it may matter more.
Two things to remember. Start from a local need, not from the goals. And test any SDG claim with one question: would a decision have been different without them?

Two exam questions. First. A council's annual report now labels its existing library opening hours as goal four, quality education. Nothing else has changed. Explain whether this is localisation of the SDGs, and outline one change that would make it so. Pause here to answer.

It isn't localisation. No decision changed, so it's SDG-washing: a label on existing activity. To localise, start from a local need. For example, if students have nowhere quiet to study after school, extend library hours on school nights, set a baseline of student use, and report it by group. The classic mistake is counting a new label as a new action.
Second. Propose how the Sustainable Development Goals could be applied to promote the health of young people in a local community. Justify your proposal. Pause here to answer.

Start with a specific community and need, and how you found it. Map it to goal three and two other goals, with mechanisms. Design components across at least three Ottawa action areas, each with a named actor, including some outside health. Give a baseline and a measure of change, by group. Say how it survives, and justify it. The classic mistake is a generic plan, with no place, no actors and no measures.

So, start from a need with the community, build on assets, act across several action areas, and measure change by group. That's our look at health in communities. Next, we turn to the body itself. Take a knee at rest, then the same knee bending into a squat. What makes that possible?
